messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: local adaptation
parts:
I was thinking about local adaptation in HMC again, and I remembered an old covariance estimator proposed by Theil and his coauthors that never really caught on in the literature but has the properties that it is always positive definite (even if columns > rows), depends only on the order statistics, and converges to the usual covariance estimator. Theil literature-reviewed himself in a short paper that can be found here

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=13846554235231786818&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

and then wrote a book about it a couple years later that is in the CU library.

I was thinking that every time the leapfrogger goes, you accumulate a quasi-sample of up to 2 * max_treedepth realizations in the neighborhood of the current parameter vector that could be used to estimate the local covariance with Theil's estimator. Since it only depends on the order statistics, the partial derivatives of that covariance matrix with respect to the parameters are all zero, so the RMHMC equations simplify back to the HMC equations.

So, if you use the previous mass matrix to leapfrog to a new proposal for the parameter vector, calculate a new proposal for the mass matrix via Theil's covariance estimator applied to the leapfrogging footprints, and do a Metropolis acceptance test for both the proposed parameter vector and the proposed mass matrix simultaneously, would you preserve all the properties you need for a Markov chain?

Thanks,
Ben

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
parts:
RMHMC only works if the metric is differentiable w.r.t. location,
which it sounds like this covariance estimator isn't. The issue is
that there are implicit updates in the generalized leapfrog integrator
that can't be satisfied otherwise.

But it also sounds like you're proposing using a fixed metric within
each trajectory, which can be done with the explicit leapfrog
integrator. However, unless you add some random perturbation to the
mass matrix you'll have a very hard time maintaining reversibility.
Even if you do, you'll wind up with a Markov chain that has a very
hard time moving between regions with different local covariance
structure, since you'll reject transitions that change the mass matrix
too much.

Detailed-balance-preserving local adaptation is tough.

Matt

On Thursday, March 7, 2013 12:45:55 AM UTC-5, Matt Hoffman wrote:
But it also sounds like you're proposing using a fixed metric within
each trajectory, which can be done with the explicit leapfrog
integrator. However, unless you add some random perturbation to the
mass matrix you'll have a very hard time maintaining reversibility.

That makes sense that it would be hard to get reversibility of the transitions if the proposed mass matrix were different from the current mass matrix. But what lead me to hope that detailed balance could still be satisfied was the overlap between the proof of detailed balance for HMC in Neal's chapter and Theil's derivation of the maximum entropy density. Neal uses the reversibility of the transitions to show that the volume of little partitions of the parameter space is preserved and then does the Metropolis thing in equation 3.8. Similarly, Theil arrives at that the density that implies that covariance estimator by partitioning up a space and then maximizing the entropy subject to the volume-preserving (and mean-preserving) constraints. So, if volume would be preserved for a fixed mass matrix and both the current and proposed mass matrices were obtained under volume-preserving constraints, I thought that might be an avenue in. But maybe there is a part to Neal's argument that hinges on more than just volume preservation that I missed?

Even if you do, you'll wind up with a Markov chain that has a very
hard time moving between regions with different local covariance
structure, since you'll reject transitions that change the mass matrix
too much.

True, but that would also be a problem without local adaptation.

Thanks,
Ben

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
parts:
Volume preservation is a soft constraint in an MCMC transition—you can
still adjust for it in the Metropolis correction if you can compute
the determinants of the Jacobians of every transition. (Cf. the recent
Lan et al. paper on Lagrangian Monte Carlo.) But reversibility is a
hard constraint—you can't satisfy detailed balance without it. The
leapfrog integrator is both volume preserving and reversible, which
makes it easy to prove correctness in HMC. (Ditto for the generalized
leapfrog, assuming the fixed-point iterations converge.)

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
parts:
Yup, reversibility is they key reason. It's pretty easy to check that
if you run one leapfrog step, negate the momentum, and run another
leapfrog step you'll wind up back where you started (except with
negative momentum). So likewise, if you run L leapfrog steps, negate
the momentum, and run another L leapfrog steps you'll again wind up
back where you started. So the procedure
1. Run L leapfrog steps with size ε
2. Negate momentum
is reversible in the sense that if you run it twice you wind up in
exactly the state you started in. So if you pretend that that
procedure is a random proposal, and plug that "distribution" (really a
delta) into the Metropolis-Hastings formula, you discover that q(θ',
m' | θ, m) = q(θ, m | θ', m'). If you didn't negate the momentum you
wouldn't have reversibility, and it'd be hard to show correctness.

Of course, in practice we generate a new momentum every iteration. But
that's really an interleaved Gibbs sampling step that's theoretically
separate from the proposal we generated using Hamiltonian dynamics.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
parts:
In HMC it doesn't matter if we negate the momentum, but it does matter
that we can. Again, a single HMC iteration consists of two updates,
each of which satisfies detailed balance individually: one Gibbs
update, and one Metropolis update. If the Metropolis update wasn't
valid then the algorithm as a whole wouldn't be valid. And the
Metropolis update isn't valid if you don't negate the momentum.

Consider the following algorithm:
1. Resample momentum
2. Simulate dynamics for L steps, accept/reject based on total energy
3. Simulate dynamics for L steps, negate momentum, accept/reject based
on total energy.
Seems a lot like HMC, right? But it's not valid, because the second
step isn't a reversible proposal--if you ran it twice, there is 0
probability that you'd wind up back where you started. And in fact, it
will give you wrong answers if you use a large enough step size that
you get rejections in step 2.

You could also imagine using an asymmetric kinetic energy function
(though I can't think why you would), and then you really would need
to implement the negation before the accept/reject step. The only
reason we can get away with not doing it is because of the symmetry of
the normal distribution (i.e., Normal(x; μ, Σ) = Normal(-x; μ, Σ)).

Matt

parts:
Just a few additional notes:

- I'd argue that the structure of the leapfrog is more important for volume preservation -- it's pretty easy to write a reversible integrator, for example the explicit Euler integrator. It's really the combination of reversibility -and- volume preservation that makes for a super-powered integrator.

- It's easier to see the need for the negation when you consider only partial momentum updates. See Section 5.5.3 of Radford's chapter.

- Odd kinetic energies would indeed be sensitive to the negation, but their trajectories are also not reversible.

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
parts:
Explicit Euler isn't reversible, is it?

And right you are, simply negating the momentum wouldn't be enough to
produce reversibility if the kinetic energy function wasn't symmetric.
You'd have to derive the algorithm differently:
1. Resample momenta
2. Sample ε_m ~ Uniform({ε, -ε}), run L leapfrog steps, accept/reject
based on total energy.
In which case you wouldn't need to worry about negating the momentum,
but you would have to be careful to choose a random direction to run
in each iteration.

Matt

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] local adaptation
parts:
Setting HMC aside for the moment, would this be a useful idea for the static mass matrix esitmation?
A
On Mar 7, 2013, at 12:21 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

I was thinking about local adaptation in HMC again, and I remembered an old covariance estimator proposed by Theil and his coauthors that never really caught on in the literature but has the properties that it is always positive definite (even if columns > rows), depends only on the order statistics, and converges to the usual covariance estimator. Theil literature-reviewed himself in a short paper that can be found here

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=13846554235231786818&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

and then wrote a book about it a couple years later that is in the CU library.

I was thinking that every time the leapfrogger goes, you accumulate a quasi-sample of up to 2 * max_treedepth realizations in the neighborhood of the current parameter vector that could be used to estimate the local covariance with Theil's estimator. Since it only depends on the order statistics, the partial derivatives of that covariance matrix with respect to the parameters are all zero, so the RMHMC equations simplify back to the HMC equations.

So, if you use the previous mass matrix to leapfrog to a new proposal for the parameter vector, calculate a new proposal for the mass matrix via Theil's covariance estimator applied to the leapfrogging footprints, and do a Metropolis acceptance test for both the proposed parameter vector and the proposed mass matrix simultaneously, would you preserve all the properties you need for a Markov chain?

Thanks,
Ben

parts: Math'll do that :)

On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 2:08 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Sorry, you're right. I was confusing the concept of "reversibility of the exact flow" with the more stringent concept of symmetry (or time-reversibility) of the numerical method. Reading back over the later chapters in Hairier, it's kind of hard to build a symmetric numerical integrator that doesn't also preserve volumes. Math is forcing itself to be awesome.
>
> On Mar 7, 2013, at 12:48 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>
>> Are we talking about the same method? By explicit Euler, I mean
>> q' <- q + ∂H/∂p
>> p' <- p - ∂H/∂q
>> where the gradients are evaluated at p, q. That's clearly not reversible.
>>
>> On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 12:45 PM, Michael Betancourt
>> <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Explicit Euler is a first order Runge-Kutta method, which are all reversible. See Chapter V of Hairer (particularly page 145).
>>>
>>> On Mar 7, 2013, at 12:39 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>>
>>>> Explicit Euler isn't reversible, is it?
>>>>
>>>> And right you are, simply negating the momentum wouldn't be enough to
>>>> produce reversibility if the kinetic energy function wasn't symmetric.
>>>> You'd have to derive the algorithm differently:
>>>> 1. Resample momenta
>>>> 2. Sample ε_m ~ Uniform({ε, -ε}), run L leapfrog steps, accept/reject
>>>> based on total energy.
>>>> In which case you wouldn't need to worry about negating the momentum,
>>>> but you would have to be careful to choose a random direction to run
>>>> in each iteration.
>>>>
>>>> Matt
>>>>
>>>> On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 12:26 PM, Michael Betancourt
>>>> <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>> Just a few additional notes:
>>>>>
>>>>> - I'd argue that the structure of the leapfrog is more important for volume preservation -- it's pretty easy to write a reversible integrator, for example the explicit Euler integrator. It's really the combination of reversibility -and- volume preservation that makes for a super-powered integrator.
>>>>>
>>>>> - It's easier to see the need for the negation when you consider only partial momentum updates. See Section 5.5.3 of Radford's chapter.
>>>>>
>>>>> - Odd kinetic energies would indeed be sensitive to the negation, but their trajectories are also not reversible.
>>>>>
>>>>> On Mar 7, 2013, at 11:41 AM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>>> In HMC it doesn't matter if we negate the momentum, but it does matter
>>>>>> that we can. Again, a single HMC iteration consists of two updates,
>>>>>> each of which satisfies detailed balance individually: one Gibbs
>>>>>> update, and one Metropolis update. If the Metropolis update wasn't
>>>>>> valid then the algorithm as a whole wouldn't be valid. And the
>>>>>> Metropolis update isn't valid if you don't negate the momentum.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Consider the following algorithm:
>>>>>> 1. Resample momentum
>>>>>> 2. Simulate dynamics for L steps, accept/reject based on total energy
>>>>>> 3. Simulate dynamics for L steps, negate momentum, accept/reject based
>>>>>> on total energy.
>>>>>> Seems a lot like HMC, right? But it's not valid, because the second
>>>>>> step isn't a reversible proposal--if you ran it twice, there is 0
>>>>>> probability that you'd wind up back where you started. And in fact, it
>>>>>> will give you wrong answers if you use a large enough step size that
>>>>>> you get rejections in step 2.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> You could also imagine using an asymmetric kinetic energy function
>>>>>> (though I can't think why you would), and then you really would need
>>>>>> to implement the negation before the accept/reject step. The only
>>>>>> reason we can get away with not doing it is because of the symmetry of
>>>>>> the normal distribution (i.e., Normal(x; μ, Σ) = Normal(-x; μ, Σ)).
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Matt
>>>>>>
>>>>>> On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 11:21 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On 3/7/13 2:09 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>>>>>> ...
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Of course, in practice we generate a new momentum every iteration. But
>>>>>>>> that's really an interleaved Gibbs sampling step that's theoretically
>>>>>>>> separate from the proposal we generated using Hamiltonian dynamics.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Thanks for the explanation, but this is exactly the bit I don't
>>>>>>> get. How does the reversibility of Hamiltonian dynamics with reversed
>>>>>>> momentum matter if we just generate a new proposal every time?
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>>
